caption: The queue food alone nearly doubled what I thought I spent. Is border-town living cheaper than the city, or does it just look that way?

slides.title:
How I spend
my R13 500
p/m income
Living in Musina
slides.body:
Female, 24
Single, shares a room with her cousin
Job: Runner for a customs clearing agent, Beitbridge border post
Net income: R13 500 p/m (this month)

slides.title: Room rent
slides.includes: Shared 2 bed room with her cousin
slides.body: It's basic, but it's five minutes from the border post, and that saves me a taxi fare twice a day.

slides.title: Transport to the border
slides.includes: Lift club fare, six days a week
slides.body: The lift club driver raises the price every time diesel does, and I never argue.

slides.title: Money home
slides.includes: My mother and two younger brothers, across the border
slides.body: It goes over on a Friday, in cash. I've never once kept a slip.

slides.title: Data & airtime
slides.includes: Calls home, the family WhatsApp group, daily
slides.body: Signal drops the moment you're off the main road, so I buy more than I should just to stay reachable.

slides.title: Food & tuckshop
slides.includes: Border post tuckshop, cooldrinks, vetkoek between queues
slides.body: I would have guessed R1 000. Standing in a queue for six hours makes you buy things.

slides.title: Everything else
slides.includes: Funeral policy, phone repayment, toiletries, a taxi to Louis Trichardt once a month
slides.body: Small things, but they're nearly a quarter of what I take home.

slides.title: What's left
slides.body: Out of R13 500. That's around R53 a day, and the border post doesn't care what day of the month it is.

slides.title: I stopped guessing
slides.body:
I uploaded my last few months to Beyond Horizon and it sorted every transaction for me.

The tuckshop total was the one I didn't want to see.

No bank login needed.
